judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 1054, which would have let public schools take on chaplains. Each school board would have had to adopt a policy letting a person volunteer or be hired as a school chaplain, saying how to apply, what qualifications were needed and what support a chaplain could give. The board would have published the chaplains' names and religious affiliation. No student could have been made to take part, no chaplain could have had authority to discipline or supervise students, and applicants would have faced the same criminal background check as any other school hire. The South Dakota House rejected it, 18-49. The bill did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 1058, which would have kept medical debt off credit reports. A medical creditor or a medical debt collector could not have reported anything about a medical debt to a consumer reporting agency, the companies that compile credit files. Breaking the rule would have been a Class 2 misdemeanor. Medical debt was defined as any debt arising from health care services or treatment. The South Dakota House rejected it, 24-44. The bill did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 1073, which would have closed voters' phone numbers and email addresses to public inspection. The county master registration file is open to the public, though social security numbers, driver license numbers and dates of birth are already withheld. The bill would have added telephone numbers and email addresses to what is withheld, and barred selling or using any of that information outside the narrow election purposes the law already allows. It would have taken effect on January 1, 2026. The South Dakota House passed it, 40-28. The South Dakota Senate never voted on it, so the bill did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 1085, which would have barred new carbon dioxide pipeline permits until federal safety rules were final. The Public Utilities Commission could not have issued a permit for a carbon dioxide pipeline until three things were true. The federal Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration had to adopt final safety rules for such pipelines. The Commission had to verify the application met those rules. Any further safety condition the Commission set had to be met. The bar would have lifted automatically once the attorney general certified the federal rules were final. The South Dakota House passed it, 40-30. The South Dakota Senate never voted on it, so the bill did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 1115, which would have made stealing a gun from a vehicle a felony carrying prison time. Entering a motor vehicle and taking a firearm or a firearm silencer would have been a Class 5 felony whatever the gun was worth. The bill also added the new crime to the list of offenses excluded from presumptive probation, the rule that otherwise sends someone convicted of a Class 5 or Class 6 felony to probation rather than prison. The South Dakota House passed it, 56-14. The South Dakota Senate never voted on it, so the bill did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 1117, which would have required hands-free use of a phone while driving. South Dakota already bars using a mobile electronic device while driving, but exempts dialing a number, taking a call and using any voice-operated or hands-free feature. The bill would have narrowed that to hands-free operation alone, so holding the phone would have been a Class 2 misdemeanor. The exemptions for emergency responders, emergency calls and navigation would have stayed. The South Dakota House rejected it, 29-39. The bill did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 1132, which would have let child care workers qualify for child care assistance. The child care assistance program helps families pay for day care, and eligibility turns on household income. The Department of Social Services would have ignored all of that income for an applicant who worked at least thirty hours a week in child care. The qualifying workplaces were a licensed day care center, a group family day care home, a registered family day care home, or a licensed before and after school program. The household still had to be under three times the federal poverty level. The South Dakota House voted 27-43 on overriding the Governor's veto, short of the 47 votes a two-thirds majority needs. The Governor vetoed the bill and the veto was not overridden, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 1201, which would have barred school staff from teaching about gender identity and required them to tell parents. A nurse, counselor, teacher, administrator or other staff member at a public or accredited private school would have had to notify a student's parent or guardian whenever gender confusion or gender dysphoria was discussed with the student. Staff could not have given any instruction about gender identity or gender expression, encouraged a student to keep such a conversation from a parent, or withheld it from a parent themselves. The South Dakota House rejected it, 28-40. The bill did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 1204, which would have freed the Legislature's audit committee to subpoena documents on its own. The Government Operations and Audit Committee reviews how state agencies spend money. It could not issue a subpoena until the Legislative Research Council's executive board ratified the decision. The bill would have deleted that approval step and stated plainly that the committee may subpoena an individual, a document, or both, and may enforce the subpoena in court. The South Dakota House passed it, 36-34. The two chambers never agreed on a final text, so the bill did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 1223, which would have created a conscience exemption from vaccines made with genetic material. The House amended the bill on the floor before the vote, narrowing it from vaccinations in general to genetic-based vaccinations. Those were defined as vaccines that work by using, modifying or transferring genetic material to produce an immune response, including messenger RNA and DNA technologies. A person could have refused one, orally or in writing, on the ground that it violated their conscience. No one could have been fired, demoted or dropped from a course for refusing, employers would have had to offer reasonable accommodations, and no state agency or public accommodation could have refused service over vaccination status. The South Dakota House rejected it, 34-36. The bill did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 1228, which would have required an environmental impact statement before any carbon dioxide pipeline permit. The Public Utilities Commission may order an environmental impact statement but does not have to. The bill would have made one compulsory before a permit for a carbon dioxide pipeline could issue, and required it to be published on the Commission's website. The bill also doubled the cap on what an applicant can be charged for reviewing the application, to one half of one percent of the first hundred million dollars of estimated construction cost. The South Dakota House rejected it, 37-32. The bill did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 1235, which would have tightened the cap on how fast property tax collections may grow. A taxing district's property tax revenue may rise each year by no more than three percent or the inflation index, whichever is lower. The bill would have cut that ceiling to two and one half percent, and applied it to school districts, which the law had exempted since 1997. Bond payments, court judgments and revenue from new construction would have stayed outside the cap. The South Dakota House passed it, 39-31. The South Dakota Senate rejected it, 13-21, so the bill did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 1242, which would have capped what a federal candidate's committee may give to state political committees. A candidate campaign committee, political action committee or political party organized under South Dakota law could not have accepted more than ten thousand dollars in a year from an authorized committee of a candidate for federal office, counting contributions and loans together. There is no such limit now. The South Dakota House passed it, 36-34. The two chambers never agreed on a final text, so the bill did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 1249, which would have let landowners sue over pressure tactics used to get carbon pipeline easements. A carbon pipeline company or its agents could not have used deception, fraud, harassment, intimidation, misrepresentation or threats to get a landowner to sign an easement. A landowner could have sued within twelve months, and a court finding such conduct would have had to void the easement and could have awarded up to three times the compensation offered as punitive damages, plus costs and legal fees. Land agents would have had to be company employees, state residents or licensed real estate agents. The South Dakota House passed it, 36-34. The South Dakota Senate rejected it, 16-18, so the bill did not become law.
